newsitem.title: FRANCE: French trucker talks inch forward, protests go on.
newsitem.headline: French trucker talks inch forward, protests go on.

text.p: Striking truck drivers tightened their stranglehold on French highways and fuel supplies with 182 roadblocks on Tuesday as they resumed talks with employers that have so far made little progress on key demands.
Union officials said the popular nine-day-old protest for wage hikes, shorter working hours and early retirement was growing in strength and putting greater pressure on the economy.
The south and west of the country were worst affected. But truckers also sealed off a petrol depot at Grigny which supplies 90 percent of petrol sold in hypermarkets in the Paris region.
The Oil Industry Association said half the nation's 175 fuel depots were blocked. Heating fuel was getting through but 500 out of 18,000 petrol stations ran dry, up from 100 on Monday.
Local authorities ordered a growing number of petrol stations around the country to supply only firemen and ambulances, or rationed sales to motorists to half a tank.
Food industry sources said 70 to 80 percent of food supplies had gone through so far and there was no panic buying, but shortages may begin if the protests went into next week.
The strike started affecting mail distribution and disrupting grain supplies to French ports.
The national traffic information centre reported trucks parked across 182 main roads across France early on Tuesday afternoon, either blocking or snarling traffic.

As a sixth round of marathon talks started just after 3 p.m. (1400 GMT), Transport Minister Bernard Pons told the National Assembly the government had offered to help meet some of the drivers' key demands by facilitating early retirement and reducing payroll taxes as an incentive to cut working hours.
"I count upon the spirit of responsibility of all to reach a very rapid settlement to this dispute," he said.
Employers' spokesman Jehan de Marne said they were ready for concessions but wage demands were unacceptable. Truckers want wage hikes and payment for hours spent waiting to load and unload.

Government mediator Robert Cros earlier reported "significant progress" with agreement in principle on changes in sick leave, travel expenses and a ban on trucks of all nationalities from French roads on Sundays.
Unions said progress was insufficient to loosen the screw.
"It is in the truckers' interest to exert maximum pressure to make employers understand that they will gain nothing by digging in their heels," said CGT leader Louis Viannet.

The French franc fell on the news that talks had stalled. Traders said fears the strike could spread, or the government could agree to the strikers' demands, weighed on the currency, pushing it below 3.39 to the German mark.

Government spokesman Alain Lamassoure asked other unions to reconsider threats to jump on the truckers' bandwagon and stage their own strikes. "It certainly isn't in the interest of road haulage employees, because some of their demands are legitimate," he told RTL radio.
FO leader Marc Blondel has threatened to extend the strike to rail and air transport unless a deal is reached by Tuesday.

The CGT has called for nationwide demonstrations and rallies at the roadblocks on Wednesday. Five rail unions urged members to support the truckers "with the appropriate means". The CFDT said widening the strike would defuse the truckers' protest.

Trade unions have announced plans for a 24-hour strike at state-owned utilities Electricite de France and Gaz de France on December 3, and for a two-day crew strike at Air France and other French airlines on Wednesday and Thursday.
